strengths: The paper addresses a clear, well-motivated gap: primate behavior recognition relies on human-centric pretrained models and single-dataset specialists. The proposed remedy — a 424-hour primate-centric pretraining dataset (PriVi) combining 11 research/observational sources with curated YouTube footage — is a substantial, reusable resource for an underserved community, with a commitment to release code, models, and most of the data.

The experimental evidence is broad and convincing on the core claim: pretraining on PriVi improves a frozen V-JEPA backbone across all four established benchmarks (ChimpACT, PanAf500, BaboonLand, ChimpBehave) and, without in-domain continual pretraining, already surpasses prior specialists (e.g., 39.25 mAP on ChimpACT vs. 31.5 for VideoPrism-g; 95.58 Acc on ChimpBehave vs. 94.62 for V-JEPA). The main conclusions therefore do not hinge on the more questionable CID protocol.

The ablation study is thorough and well-designed: dataset composition (Table 2, YT-Filtered vs. YT-Random vs. R&O), primate-centric cropping during pretraining (Table 5), and attentive classifier design (downprojection, class tokens, depth) are each isolated. Notably, the 220k-parameter frozen classifier outperforms the 49.6M-parameter V-JEPA 2 readout, a practically useful finding for the low-label regime.

The method is compute-efficient and reproducible: only 75k pretraining steps (~8 epochs, ~11 hours on 4 A100s), lightweight head, fixed evaluation protocols with five classifier seeds and multi-view test-time averaging, reducing noise on small datasets.

The curation pipeline (CLIP-embedding relevance classifier with reported precision/recall/ROC-AUC, Grounding DINO detection filtering with 82.7 mAP on PanAf500, metadata-driven subsampling) is documented with enough quantitative detail to assess its quality, and the ablations show each pipeline component contributes (Table 2).
weaknesses: The in-domain continual pretraining (CID) protocol raises a potential leakage concern: the model is continually pretrained on unlabeled ChimpACT/PanAf500 videos and then evaluated on validation sets of the same datasets. Even without labels, the encoder has seen the very clips (and near-duplicate frames of them) used for evaluation, which may inflate the reported gains (e.g., +2.68 mAP on ChimpACT, +7.34 B-Acc on PanAf500 in Table 3, and the best results in Table 4 all use CID). The paper does not discuss or control for this overlap, and it is unclear whether validation/test footage is excluded from CID. This should be addressed explicitly.

All ablations and many headline numbers are reported on validation sets rather than held-out test splits, and model selection (best validation accuracy on ChimpACT/PanAf500) plus learning-rate sweeps for ablations occur on the same data. BaboonLand and ChimpBehave lack validation splits, so their numbers are reported end-of-training; protocol differences across datasets make cross-dataset comparisons less clean.

Baseline comparisons mix numbers from original papers with incompatible protocols and the authors' own reproduction (AlphaChimp), and some comparisons are fragmented: e.g., VideoPrism-g is only reported on ChimpACT, ChimpVLM only on ChimpACT, VideoMAEv2 only on BaboonLand/ChimpBehave. A complete, unified re-evaluation of at least the strongest frozen baselines (VideoPrism-g, VideoMAEv2) under the identical protocol would strengthen the SOTA claim considerably.

The dataset composition is skewed relative to the evaluation tasks: 43% of PriVi is macaques (63% in YT-Filtered) while all four benchmarks involve chimpanzees and baboons. The ablations partially address this, but a per-species or per-domain contribution analysis (beyond the YT/R&O split) is missing, and the paper itself concedes only 11 research setups are covered.

14% of the pretraining data (a camera-trap source dataset) cannot be released, which limits exact reproducibility of the headline model; the justification (ongoing research) is reasonable but means the strongest configuration cannot be fully rebuilt by others.

Presentation issues, while minor, should be fixed: several typos ('pertraining', 'surprisingly' misspelled, 'our datasets sets a new baseline', 'several modern approached'), and the evaluation-protocol details (which split is used for ablation vs. comparison, exact handling of CID data splits) would benefit from a dedicated paragraph. These are correctable and do not undermine the contribution.

strengths: The PriVi dataset (424 hours of primate-centric video assembled from 11 research settings plus curated YouTube footage) is a substantial and genuinely useful community resource for a data-scarce domain; the composition analysis in Table 1 adds transparency.

The paper demonstrates consistent improvements over a strong frozen V-JEPA baseline across four benchmarks (Table 2), and the ablations are well-designed: dataset composition (YT-Filtered vs. YT-Random vs. R&O), continual in-domain pretraining (Table 3), primate-centric cropping, and attentive classifier design choices (Table 5) are each individually justified.

The narrow attentive classifier (220k parameters) is a practical contribution; the finding that it outperforms much larger heads (Table 5) supports the frozen-evaluation paradigm for small animal behavior datasets.

The continual pretraining (CID) result is interesting and useful: it shows that unlabeled in-domain video adds further gains without labels, which matches the realistic constraints of behavioral research.

The paper is generally well written and organized, and the data curation pipeline (relevance classifier, zero-shot detection filtering, metadata-driven subsampling) is reproducible in spirit and reported with concrete metrics (precision/recall, mAP).
weaknesses: The abstract claims the approach 'scales favorably with fewer labels,' but no label-efficiency experiment (e.g., performance vs. number of labeled samples) appears anywhere in the manuscript. This is a headline claim without supporting evidence, which is a material weakness rather than a presentation issue.

Overclaiming relative to the evidence: Section 5.2 states that PriVi+CID 'surpasses the state of the art on all four datasets across both class-balanced and unbalanced metrics,' yet Table 4 shows PriVi+CID degrades PanAf500 Acc (86.74 -> 85.01) relative to PriVi alone, and PriVi alone is already below the VideoMAEv2 baseline entry on the BaboonLand columns (92.3/74.8 vs. 75.43/33.99, depending on column alignment). The text does not match the table.

Internal inconsistencies undermine confidence in the numbers: the V-JEPA baseline in Table 4 (ChimpACT mAP 30.85, PanAf500 Acc 81.96, B-Acc 60.19) differs from the same baseline in Table 2 (32.00, 84.70, 71.95) with no explanation of the differing evaluation setup.

Baseline comparisons in Table 4 are incomplete and difficult to compare against: many rows have missing entries (ChimpVLM, AlphaChimp, VideoPrism-g, InternVideo-L cover only a subset of datasets), AlphaChimp uses the authors' own reproduction 'due to incompatible evaluation protocols,' and the VideoMAEv2 row placement is ambiguous. The claim of surpassing 'fully finetuned baselines' therefore rests on a sparse and partly non-standard comparison.

Potential data leakage is not discussed: PriVi includes YouTube footage of primates, and evaluation datasets are zoo/camera-trap recordings of well-known populations; the possibility that pretraining data overlaps with evaluation content (same zoos, sites, or individuals) is neither checked nor addressed.

All experiments rely on ground-truth annotated bounding boxes at evaluation time (acknowledged in Limitations), which weakens the 'general-purpose model for the wild' framing; the zero-shot detector is used only during pretraining.

Reproducibility is partially compromised: 14% of the pretraining data (a camera trap source dataset) cannot be released, so the full dataset and exact pretraining mixture cannot be reconstructed by others.

The classifier ablation interpretation is somewhat overstated: the 'w/o downproject' baseline performing worse (Table 5) may reflect training difficulty of large heads on small datasets rather than a fundamental design advantage, and the paper itself varies learning rates to compensate without reporting per-ablation tuning details.

Numerous typos and minor errors ('PRIMA+CID' instead of PriVi+CID, 'pertraining,' 'sub-datset,' 'surprised,' 'our datasets sets a new baseline') suggest insufficient proofreading, and Figure 1's R&O relevance/diversity annotations are only loosely connected to the described pipeline.

strengths: The paper makes a genuine data-centric contribution: a 424-hour primate-centric video pretraining dataset assembled from 11 research settings plus curated web footage, addressing a real gap since existing large animal video datasets contain few or no primates.

The data curation pipeline (cut detection, CLIP-based relevance filtering with reported precision/recall/ROC-AUC of 82.8/90.3/95.9, zero-shot Grounding DINO primate detection with 82.7 mAP on PanAf500 detection) is described concretely and quantitatively, supporting reproducibility.

The evaluation is reasonably broad, spanning four heterogeneous primate behavior benchmarks (camera trap, zoo, drone footage, multi-label spatio-temporal), with consistent improvements over the V-JEPA baseline across all of them.

The ablation study is thorough and informative: it cleanly separates the contribution of YT-Filtered vs. R&O vs. their combination (Table 2), shows curated selection beats random YouTube selection, demonstrates primate-centric cropping matters substantially (e.g., 38.75 vs. 32.62 mAP on ChimpACT), and justifies each component of the compact 220k-parameter attentive classifier against much larger alternatives (Table 5).

The finding that broad domain pretraining outperforms continual pretraining on a single in-domain dataset, and that no cross-dataset transfer is observed between ChimpACT and PanAf500, is a useful empirical insight for the community.

The lightweight frozen attentive classifier (220k parameters) outperforming finetuned models with orders of magnitude more parameters (e.g., ChimpVLM at 167M) is practically relevant for the low-label regime common in behavioral ecology.
The paper is well organized and clearly written, with an honest limitations section acknowledging dataset scope and the reliance on ground-truth bounding boxes.
weaknesses: The continual pretraining (CID) protocol uses unlabeled video from the target evaluation datasets, which is a transductive setting that is not directly comparable to the prior baselines in Table 4 (X3D, VideoMAEv2, ChimpVLM, etc.), none of which use target-dataset video. The headline claim of surpassing the state of the art partly rests on this additional unlabeled in-domain data.

The abstract claims the approach 'scales favorably with fewer labels' and benefits low-label applications, but no label-efficiency experiments (e.g., accuracy vs. number of labeled samples curves) are reported anywhere in the manuscript; this claim is unsupported by the presented evidence.

Ablation results are reported only on validation sets, and best-checkpoint selection is based on validation accuracy for ChimpACT and PanAf500; BaboonLand and ChimpBehave lack validation splits, so some results may be optimistically biased and the comparability of the ablation setup across datasets is imperfect.

The baseline comparison in Table 4 is incomplete and uneven: VideoPrism-g is reported for only one metric on one dataset, InternVideo-L and VideoMAEv2 cover only two datasets, and the AlphaChimp comparison is a self-reproduction under a modified protocol. The 'outperforms prior work on all four datasets' claim would be more convincing with complete, protocol-matched comparisons.

The headline SOTA framing is somewhat overstated: on ChimpACT, PriVi+CID has lower unweighted accuracy than PriVi alone (84.93 vs. 89.65) and the gains on some metrics are modest, so 'surpasses the state of the art on all four datasets across both class-balanced and unbalanced metrics' does not hold uniformly.

14% of the pretraining data (the camera trap source dataset) cannot be released, which weakens full reproducibility of the exact PriVi composition; the abstract's 'majority of the dataset' phrasing is accurate but should be weighed against the central role of the dataset contribution.
The dataset is heavily skewed toward macaques (43.0%) while the evaluation datasets cover chimpanzees and baboons; a composition ablation addressing this imbalance is absent.

No variance measures, confidence intervals, or multiple random seeds for pretraining are reported; the five-classifier averaging mitigates classifier-initiation noise but not pretraining stochasticity.

Minor presentation issues: several typos ('pertraining', 'datasets sets a new baseline', 'suprisingly'), and the typo 'PRIMA+CID' in Section 5.2 where 'PriVi+CID' is meant, which could confuse readers about the method name.
